Michael Burry Swaps MU, NBIS, NVDA, PLTR Shorts For Puts — Says AI Bubble May Burst ‘Sooner Than Later’

Trading disclosure

Burry covered his common-stock shorts in MU, NBIS, CAT, SOXX, CRWV, NVDA, and PLTR.

He replaced the short positions with puts across several names, with many extending into 2027.

Burry said tax-loss harvesting played a role, but most of the repositioning came after weekend research on the AI bubble.

"The Big Short" investor Michael Burry has repositioned his portfolio after weekend research prompted him to move his timelines forward, replacing his short common-stock positions with put options. He also opened a new short position in MetLife and said most of the repositioning was driven by his belief that the AI bubble may burst "sooner than later."

Burry Replaces Short Positions With Puts

"As of today, put options completely replaced my short positions," Burry wrote in a post on Substack.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

He said he covered all his short common-stock positions in Micron (MU), Nebius (NBIS), Caterpillar (CAT), iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), CoreWeave (CRWV), Nvidia (NVDA) and Palantir (PLTR).

Burry replaced the Micron short with puts at the June expiry and in the $500 strike price range. He replaced the Nebius short with June puts in the double-digit strike price range, while the Caterpillar short was replaced with December 2027 puts around the $400 strike price.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF short was replaced with September 2027 puts struck in the low $400s.

Burry also replaced and rolled his Palantir short and put position into an enlarged put position concentrated at the September 2027 expiry, with strikes in the low $100s. He replaced the Nvidia short with September 2027 puts at strikes in the mid $100s.

Burry Adds New MetLife Short

Burry said he initiated one new short position in MetLife (MET) "with LEAP puts out several years struck in the $70s."

He also covered his Oracle (ORCL) short and replaced it with December 2027 expiry puts at strikes in the mid-double digits.

Burry said he covered the CoreWeave short but has "as yet" been unable to acquire puts at an attractive price.

Burry said he folded his QQQ put position into an enlarged and rolled Nasdaq 100 Index put position. The September 2027 strikes are in the $24,000s, he said.

AI Bubble Could Burst 'Sooner Than Later'

Burry said some of the repositioning was motivated by "tax loss harvesting," but added that the "majority of it was motivated by research this past weekend." That research, he said, led him to believe "the bubble in AI may burst sooner than later."

By Karen Roman

Cyber intelligence and technology provider REDL Intermediate Holdings, LLC (REDLattice) said it is going public through a combination with Bold Eagle Acquisition Corp. (Nasdaq: BEAG) and will trade on Nasdaq under the ticker "REDL" by the end of 2026.

The transaction values REDLattice at $1.25 billion and is could produce up to $610 million of gross proceeds, including $335 million of committed capital from new and existing mutual fund and institutional investors, and up to $275 million from Bold Eagle's trust account assuming no redemptions, the company said.

"REDLattice was built to provide the U.S. and its allies with a decisive technical edge against the world's most sophisticated adversaries, at a moment when artificial intelligence has fundamentally accelerated the pace of cyber conflict," said CEO Andy Boyd.

REDLattice will use the proceeds from the combination to refinance all its existing debt, to fund the final cash earnout payment from the company's previous acquisition of Paragon Solutions Ltd., and to invest in organic growth, product expansion, and M&A, it said.

title: Palantir Did Not Win the FAA Contract for SMART. Time to Buy the Stock Anyway?
detail:
Palantir Did Not Win the FAA Contract for SMART. Time to Buy the Stock Anyway?
Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Mon, September 28, 2026 at 10:13 AM MDT 3 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) just announced plans to roll out a new AI-based system it calls Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART.

Consequently, analysts at firms such as Rosenblatt turned their attention to Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), believing SMART could become an additional revenue source for the software-as-a-service (SaaS) stock. Palantir did not win the contract, but investors likely would have had trouble benefiting from this new business line -- here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Palantir and SMART

Admittedly, Palantir was well positioned to implement a system like SMART. The company's tools could have improved SMART by making air traffic management more efficient and averting potential problems. Nonetheless, despite those attributes, the 12-year, $875 million deal went to a company called Air Space Intelligence.

Unfortunately, even if Palantir had won the contract, investors faced one critical obstacle -- the current state of Palantir. The company's stock trades at a P/E ratio of 164, and even its forward P/E reduces the earnings multiple to just 119. When also factoring in a sales multiple of 80 and a price-to-book value ratio of 47, the stock appears priced to perfection by just about every measure.

Also, while its growth is robust, it may not be enough to justify its valuation premium. In the first half of 2026, its nearly $3.6 billion in revenue increased by 89% compared with the same period in 2025. Also, it earned $1.9 billion during the same period compared with $541 million in the same year-ago time frame.

Palantir's stock stood still amid the lost contract. However, since the market has bid its stock price into the stratosphere, bad news from a variety of sources could still trigger selling. Knowing that, investors may want to think twice about buying the stock.

Moving forward with Palantir

Given its valuation, Palantir shareholders would have likely not benefited from the SMART contract even if the FAA had awarded it to Palantir. Indeed, winning the SMART contract would likely have been yet another validation of the power of Palantir's software.

Unfortunately, Palantir's growth has become a known quantity, and the stock supports valuations that confirm its growth potential. Its high valuation increases the odds that this potential revenue source will not help Palantir stock, and investors could face a sell-off should any bad news spook them.

SoundHound AI SOUN and BigBear.ai Holdings BBAI offer investors two very different ways to gain exposure to artificial intelligence. SoundHound is building voice, conversational and agentic AI solutions across enterprises, automobiles, restaurants and financial services, while BigBear.ai focuses on mission-ready AI for defense, national security, logistics and other secure environments.

Both remain high-growth, loss-making AI companies and both have suffered substantial share-price declines in 2026. However, their latest operating trends are diverging, particularly in revenue growth, earnings-estimate revisions and product expansion.

Let's dive deep and closely compare the fundamentals of the two stocks to determine which one is a better investment now.

The Case for SoundHound Stock

SoundHound's growth profile strengthened considerably in the second quarter. Revenues jumped 45% year over year to a record $61.9 million, while GAAP gross margin expanded 610 basis points to 45.1%. Adjusted EBITDA loss improved to $9.6 million from $14.3 million a year earlier, showing that rapid top-line expansion is beginning to generate operating leverage.

OASYS, SoundHound's self-learning agentic AI platform, is becoming an important growth driver. The company is gaining traction across healthcare, banking, automotive and restaurants, while partnerships are expanding its distribution. Its opportunities also extend beyond cloud-based enterprise AI. On Sept. 24, SoundHound introduced OASYS Edge, allowing LLM-powered voice agents to operate directly on vehicles and smart devices, including without continuous connectivity.

The recently completed LivePerson acquisition materially broadens this opportunity. SoundHound now reaches customers that include 25 of the Fortune 100 and has a portfolio of more than 750 patents. Integrating LivePerson's digital-messaging infrastructure with OASYS creates an omnichannel offering spanning voice, web, mobile, SMS and social channels. SoundHound also said the combined existing customer base could represent more than $500 million in future revenues, although realizing that opportunity will depend on successful integration and cross-selling.

Still, SoundHound remains unprofitable. The company reported a $42.8 million GAAP net loss in the second quarter, and integrating LivePerson adds execution risk. Its rapid acquisition-driven expansion also makes cost discipline and progress toward sustainable profitability important factors to watch.

CorpGov hosted the second LA CorpGov Forum on Sept. 18, 2026, at The Huntington Library in San Marino, California. This event brought together members of the financial community from both LA and beyond in panels focused on the finance of entertainment and media, sports, along with capital markets and shareholder activism.

Panel: Capital Markets Assessment and IPO Readiness ​

Nicolle Brady, Managing Director, Protiviti ​​

Joseph Fish, CEP, Managing Director, Stock Operations, Infinite Equity

Jeff Meyer, Managing Director, Protiviti ​

Ramey Layne, Partner, Capital Markets and Mergers & Acquisitions, Vinson & Elkins

Josh Waldron, Interim CFO, Scale AI

Main Topics of Discussion: 

IPO markets are highly active and relatively issuer-friendly, with panelists noting that first-half 2026 IPO volume was roughly three times the first half of 2025, excluding SpaceX; investors, however, appear increasingly focused on profitability, risk controls and a credible path to sustainable performance.

IPO readiness requires early preparation. Companies need mature systems, internal controls, financial reporting processes, governance structures and experienced teams well before going public.

AI is reshaping the IPO process, from investor-relations preparation and roadshows to financial close and technical accounting. Panelists said AI can accelerate data analysis and drafting, but human oversight remains essential because AI-generated work can introduce errors and governance risks.

Dual-class share structures are becoming more common, particularly among large, founder-led and high-growth companies. Panelists noted that roughly one-third of larger IPOs discussed had dual-class structures, compared with about 20% several years ago, with sunset provisions sometimes used as a compromise with institutional investors.

Going public involves significant trade-offs. Beyond potentially raising capital and providing liquidity, companies face substantial costs, regulatory obligations, greater board oversight, dilution considerations and pressure to respond to public investors and analysts—making remaining private an important alternative for some companies.
